hints: Think about which bond in 2-methylpropene is electron rich and how it can act towards the slightly positive H in $\text{H-Cl}$.
Remember to show the polarity on $\text{H-Cl}$ and consider what species is left after $\text{H}^{+}$ adds to the double bond.
Consider what the $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ion formed in the first step can do towards the positively charged carbon in the second step.
walkthrough:
Spot the electrophile in H-Cl**
$\text{H-Cl}$ is polar because $\text{Cl}$ is more electronegative than $\text{H}$, so write it as $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$. The $\text{C=C}$ double bond in $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$ is an area of high electron density, so it acts as a nucleophile and attacks the $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ end.

Make the first curly arrow and form the carbocation**
Draw a curly arrow starting at the $\text{C=C}$ double bond and pointing to the $\text{H}$ of $\text{H-Cl}$. At the same time the $\text{H-Cl}$ bond breaks, with its pair of electrons moving onto $\text{Cl}$ to form $\text{Cl}^{-}$. The $\text{H}$ joins the $\text{CH}_{2}$ end to give $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{+}$. This is a tertiary carbocation with the positive charge on the central carbon.

Attack by chloride ion to finish the product**
Now you have a $\text{C}^{+}$ and a $\text{Cl}^{-}$ with lone pairs. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Cl}^{-}$ to the $\text{C}^{+}$ centre. This forms the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond and gives 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CCl}$.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{H}^{\delta+}-\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$ shown with dipole. Curly arrow from $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ and $\text{H-Cl}$ bond breaks to $\text{Cl}^{-}$.
Intermediate: $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{+}$, tert-butyl cation, with positive charge on central C.
Step 2: Curly arrow from $\text{H-Cl}$ bonding pair to $\text{Cl}$ to give $\text{Cl}^{-}$ with 3 lone pairs, then curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{Cl}^{-}$ to $\text{C}^{+}$ to give $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{CCl}$.

hints: Compare the two possible carbocations that could form when $\text{H}^{+}$ adds to the two different carbons of the $\text{C=C}$ bond.
Recall how alkyl methyl groups attached directly to a $\text{C}^{+}$ centre affect its stability.
walkthrough:
Picture the two competing routes**
If $\text{H}^{+}$ adds to the $\text{C(CH}_{3})_{2}$ end you get a primary $\text{C}^{+}$, $\text{(CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}^{+}$. If $\text{H}^{+}$ adds to the $\text{CH}_{2}$ end you get a tertiary $\text{C}^{+}$, $\text{(CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{+}$. The product you get depends on which intermediate forms.

Link alkyl groups to stability**
Alkyl groups push electron density towards the $\text{C}^{+}$ by the positive inductive effect. The tertiary ion has three methyl groups directly attached to the $\text{C}^{+}$, so it gets much more electron donation than the primary ion with only one alkyl group. That extra donation spreads and stabilises the positive charge, so the tertiary route is lower in energy and gives the major product.

Final answer: The tertiary carbocation $(\text{CH}_{3})_{3}\text{C}^{+}$ leading to 2-chloro-2-methylpropane is more stable than the primary carbocation leading to 1-chloro-2-methylpropane.
This is due to the greater positive inductive effect from 3 methyl / alkyl groups attached to the $\text{C}^{+}$ centre, which donate electron density and stabilise the positive charge.

hints: Think about what happens when a halogenoalkane $\text{R-X}$ is warmed with aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol, what replaces the halogen.
Recall the name for a reaction where one atom or group is swapped for another, in this case $\text{X}$ for $\text{OH}$ from water.
walkthrough:
Work out what T must be**
Both $\text{Q}$ and $\text{M}$ are $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{X}$ and both give the same organic product $\text{T}$ plus $\text{X}^{-}$ which precipitates with $\text{Ag}^{+}$. That tells you $\text{X}$ has been replaced by $\text{OH}$ from water. So $\text{T}$ is an alcohol, $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{OH}$, containing the hydroxyl functional group.

Name the reaction type**
One group, halogen, is directly swapped for another group, $\text{OH}$. Swapping one group for another is substitution. Because water provides the $\text{OH}$, it is also called hydrolysis, and mechanistically it is nucleophilic substitution.

Final answer: functional group in T: hydroxyl / alcohol / $\text{OH}$
type of reaction: (nucleophilic) substitution / hydrolysis

hints: Use Table 4.1 to identify which halide ion gives a yellow precipitate with $\text{Ag}^{+}$(aq).
walkthrough:
Translate colour into ion**
Yellow precipitate with $\text{AgNO}_{3}$(aq) is the classic test for iodide. $\text{M}$ gives yellow, so $\text{M}$ releases $\text{I}^{-}$. The precipitate forms when $\text{I}^{-}$ meets $\text{Ag}^{+}$, so the ionic equation is $$\text{I}^{-} + \text{Ag}^{+} \rightarrow \text{AgI}$$ Include state symbols if you wish as (aq) + (aq) to (s).

hints: Recall that white $\text{AgCl}$ means Q contains $\text{Cl}$ and yellow $\text{AgI}$ means M contains $\text{I}$, then compare $\text{C-Cl}$ and $\text{C-I}$ bond strengths.
walkthrough:
Connect bond strength to speed**
Precipitate appears only after the $\text{C-X}$ bond breaks to release $\text{X}^{-}$. $\text{C-I}$ is longer and weaker than $\text{C-Cl}$, so it needs less energy to break. Therefore the iodoalkane $\text{M}$ hydrolyses faster than the chloroalkane $\text{Q}$ and its yellow $\text{AgI}$ precipitate appears more quickly.
Final answer: reagent M, because $\text{C-I}$ bond is weaker than $\text{C-Cl}$ bond so hydrolyses more quickly to release $\text{I}^{-}$.

hints: Remember that alkaline $\text{I}_{2}$(aq) giving a yellow precipitate means a positive triiodomethane test, which tells you T contains a $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)}$ group and the rest of the molecule becomes a carboxylate anion.
walkthrough:
Use the triiodomethane clue backwards**
Alkaline $\text{I}_{2}$ giving a yellow precipitate of $\text{CHI}_{3}$ is positive for $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)}-$ . Since $\text{T}$ is $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{OH}$ and gives this test, $\text{T}$ must be $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. Oxidative cleavage removes the $\text{CH}_{3}$ part as $\text{CHI}_{3}$ and leaves the remaining three carbons as the carboxylate, $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{COO}^{-}$$ which is propanoate.

hints: Combine the facts that M is a straight chain $\text{C}_{4}$ iodoalkane and that hydrolysis of M gives butan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$.
Think about where the I must have been in M for direct substitution of I by OH to give the OH on carbon 2.
walkthrough:
Fix the carbon skeleton and halogen**
From (b)(ii), $\text{M}$ gives $\text{AgI}$, so $\text{X = I}$. It has formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{I}$ and is straight chain, so the backbone is four carbons in a row.

Place the I to match T**
Hydrolysis simply swaps $\text{I}$ for $\text{OH}$ at the same carbon. From (b)(iv), $\text{T}$ is butan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, with $\text{OH}$ on carbon 2. Therefore $\text{I}$ must also have been on carbon 2 in $\text{M}$. So $\text{M}$ is $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHICH}_{3}$$ drawn clearly as $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH(I)}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}_{3}$.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHICH}_{3}$
Unambiguous displayed or skeletal structure of straight chain 2-iodobutane with I on carbon 2: $\text{CH}_{3}-\text{CH(I)}-\text{CH}_{2}-\text{CH}_{3}$
